topic: Three-tier data classification: public, internal, confidential
scope_note: A common generic three-tier scheme for employees: what each class means, everyday examples, handling, who classifies, and what to do when unsure. No company policy was supplied, so no organisation-specific rules, tools, laws, fines or statistics.

facts.statement: Data classification sorts information into a small number of classes according to how much harm disclosure would cause, so that each class can carry its own handling rules.
facts.reference_hint: ISO/IEC 27002 control on classification of information; NIST SP 800-60 and FIPS 199 (impact levels)

facts.statement: Public information is approved for release to anyone outside the organisation, so its disclosure causes no harm.
facts.caveat: Wording varies by organisation; published university and government policies define the lowest class in this way. Say 'in a typical scheme'.
facts.reference_hint: Published university and government classification policies

facts.statement: Internal information is meant for employees and other authorised staff, and its disclosure would cause only limited harm.
facts.caveat: Some schemes call this class 'private' or 'for internal use'. Say 'in a typical scheme'.
facts.reference_hint: Published university and government classification policies

facts.statement: Confidential information is restricted to the people who need it for their work, and its disclosure could cause significant harm.
facts.caveat: Wording varies by organisation. Say 'in a typical scheme'.
facts.reference_hint: Published university and government classification policies

facts.statement: Class names, the number of classes and the exact rules differ between organisations, so the organisation's own policy overrides a generic description.
facts.reference_hint: ISO/IEC 27002 leaves the scheme design to the organisation

facts.statement: Everyday public examples are a published press release, a job advert already posted, and the content of the public marketing website.
facts.caveat: Examples illustrate a typical scheme; the organisation's policy decides each case.
facts.reference_hint: Typical examples in published university and government policies

facts.statement: Everyday internal examples are team meeting notes, the organisation chart and internal procedures.
facts.caveat: Examples illustrate a typical scheme; some organisations publish their org chart, so the policy decides.
facts.reference_hint: Typical examples in published university and government policies

facts.statement: Everyday confidential examples are payroll and salary data, customers' personal data, contracts and unreleased financial results.
facts.caveat: Examples illustrate a typical scheme; the organisation's policy decides each case.
facts.reference_hint: Typical examples in published university and government policies

facts.statement: An item's class is decided by its content and by the harm its disclosure could cause, not by its file format, its location or how convenient it is to share.
facts.caveat: Phrased as common guidance, not a quotation from one standard.
facts.reference_hint: ISO/IEC 27002 and NIST SP 800-60 base classification on impact of disclosure

facts.statement: Information is public only once someone with authority has approved its release; looking harmless is not approval.
facts.caveat: Who approves release (communications team, owner) depends on the organisation.
facts.reference_hint: Published university and government classification policies

facts.statement: The class label belongs to the information and travels with it, so a document keeps its class whether it is on paper, in a file, in a message or on a screen.
facts.caveat: How labels are applied (header, file name, metadata, stamp) depends on the organisation; the lesson stays generic.
facts.reference_hint: ISO/IEC 27002 control on labelling of information

facts.statement: Public information can be shared outside the organisation freely, once it has been approved for release.
facts.caveat: Typical handling; the organisation's policy governs.
facts.reference_hint: Published university and government classification policies

facts.statement: Internal information stays among employees and authorised staff, and is not posted or sent outside the organisation without approval.
facts.caveat: Typical handling; sharing with a partner under contract or approval is an organisation-specific rule.
facts.reference_hint: Published university and government classification policies

facts.statement: Confidential information goes only to named people who need it, and is shared only through approved, protected channels.
facts.caveat: Which channels are approved is organisation-specific; the lesson names none.
facts.reference_hint: Published university and government classification policies; ISO/IEC 27002 handling of information

facts.statement: Confidential information is normally stored in approved locations with access limited to those who need it, and is commonly encrypted when stored and sent.
facts.caveat: Encryption expectations vary by organisation and by scheme; say 'commonly expected'.
facts.reference_hint: Published university and government classification policies

facts.statement: The higher the class, the more careful the disposal: confidential paper is shredded and confidential files are securely deleted, not left in ordinary bins.
facts.caveat: Typical practice; exact disposal methods are set by the organisation.
facts.reference_hint: Published university and government classification policies

facts.statement: The information owner, usually the person or team who creates the information or is accountable for it, is responsible for deciding its class.
facts.caveat: Who counts as owner (creator, manager, data owner) varies by organisation; the lesson stays generic.
facts.reference_hint: ISO/IEC 27002: information is classified by its owner

facts.statement: When unsure how to classify something, treat it as the higher class and ask the information owner.
facts.caveat: Common guidance in published classification policies, not a quotation from one standard. Who to ask depends on the organisation.
facts.reference_hint: Published university and government classification policies

facts.statement: The United States federal FIPS standard on security categorisation sets low, moderate and high impact levels by the harm of disclosure, which is the harm-based logic that a three-tier scheme follows.
facts.caveat: That standard covers federal systems and also integrity and availability. It is a parallel framing of harm, not a one-to-one match with public, internal and confidential. Cite only as background.

terms.meaning: The person or team accountable for a piece of information, who decides its class.
Access is limited to people who need the information to do their work.
One of the three levels: public, internal, confidential; also called a label or tier.

not_claimed: No breach statistics, costs or fines.
No specific law or regulator is named as the requirement behind any class.
No claim that every organisation uses exactly these three classes; many add a further top class such as restricted, which this lesson does not present as part of the scheme.
No claim that internal means harmless, or that anything not marked confidential is safe to share.
No claim that a document's class depends on its format, or that digital files need a label but paper does not.
No company tool names, channel names or contact names.
No quotations attributed to any standard or person.
No claim that encryption is required by every scheme for every confidential item.
